references.notes: Link changed from the OUP article page (audit: returns only a navigation shell to automated reads) to the IDSA-hosted PDF of the same guideline, which was the copy read this run; duplicate ref 9 (same PDF) removed. WebFetch returns quotes in fragments of up to 125 characters; where a clause was summarized rather than quoted by the tool it is noted on the claim. Scite verify_papers verified the DOI (Scite labels the record "Executive Summary", a metadata quirk) and flagged one contrasting citation (10.1007/s10096-017-3001-0) reporting blood culture positivity of 4-9% in other studies; the page therefore attributes the 5% figure to the IDSA and says "generally".

claims.text: Most cellulitis arises from streptococci, often group A; S. aureus causes cellulitis less often (key takeaway)
claims.quote: the vast majority of these infections arise from streptococci, often group A, but also from other groups, [...] Staphylococcus aureus less frequently causes cellulitis,

claims.text: Typical cellulitis without systemic signs: antibiotic active against streptococci; suitable oral choices penicillin, amoxicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, dicloxacillin, cephalexin, clindamycin (key takeaway, first-line table intro, table notes, citable summary)
claims.quote: Typical cases of cellulitis without systemic signs of infection should receive an antimicrobial agent that is active against streptococci (mild; Figure 1) (strong, moderate).

claims.text: Suitable oral antibiotics for most patients; many can take oral medication from the start
claims.quote: A large percentage of patients can receive oral medications from the start for typical cellulitis [...] suitable antibiotics for most patients include penicillin, amoxicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, dicloxacillin, cephalexin, or clindamycin.

claims.text: MRSA situations: penetrating trauma, MRSA infection elsewhere, nasal colonization, injection drug use, purulent drainage, SIRS (key takeaway, MRSA list)
claims.quote: For patients whose cellulitis is associated with penetrating trauma, evidence of MRSA infection elsewhere, nasal colonization with MRSA, injection drug use, purulent drainage, or SIRS (severe nonpurulent),

claims.text: MRSA is an unusual cause of typical cellulitis, so most cases do not need MRSA coverage
claims.quote: MRSA is an unusual cause of typical cellulitis. [...] suggesting that cellulitis due to MRSA is uncommon and treatment for that organism is usually unnecessary

claims.text: Oral options covering both streptococci and MRSA: clindamycin alone, or TMP-SMX or doxycycline with a beta-lactam such as cephalexin (key takeaway, MRSA table, sidebar, citable summary)
claims.quote: If coverage for both streptococci and MRSA is desired for oral therapy, options include clindamycin alone or the combination of either SMX-TMP or doxycycline with a β-lactam (eg, penicillin, cephalexin, or amoxicillin).

claims.text: TMP-SMX and doxycycline are IDSA oral options for MRSA
claims.quote: or oral therapy with doxycycline, clindamycin, or SMX-TMP.

claims.text: Adult oral doses: cephalexin 500 mg four times daily; dicloxacillin 500 mg four times daily; amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily; clindamycin 300-450 mg four times daily; doxycycline 100 mg twice daily; TMP-SMX 1-2 DS tablets twice daily
claims.quote: Cephalexin 500 mg qid po [...] Dicloxacillin 500 mg qid po [...] Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg bid po [...] 300–450 mg qid po [...] 100 mg bid po [...] 1–2 doublestrength tablets bid po

claims.text: 5-day course, extended if not improved (tables, duration paragraph, sidebar, citable summary)
claims.quote: The recommended duration of antimicrobial therapy is 5 days, but treatment should be extended if the infection has not improved within this time period (strong, high).

claims.text: Outpatient treatment recommended only for patients without SIRS, altered mental status, or hemodynamic instability (systemic symptoms paragraph, citable summary)
claims.quote: Outpatient therapy is recommended for patients who do not have SIRS, altered mental status, or hemodynamic instability

claims.text: Hospitalization recommended when deeper or necrotizing infection is suspected, in severe immunocompromise, or when outpatient treatment is failing (classification callout, citable summary)
claims.quote: Hospitalization is recommended if there is concern for a deeper or necrotizing infection, for patients with poor adherence to therapy, for infection in a severely immunocompromised patient,

claims.text: Classification: mild = no purulence and no systemic signs; moderate = systemic signs, systemic antibiotics indicated
claims.quote: Moderate infection: typical cellulitis/erysipelas with systemic signs of infection. [...] For cellulitis with systemic signs of infection (moderate nonpurulent; Figure 1), systemic antibiotics are indicated.

claims.text: Severe = failed oral treatment, SIRS (temperature above 38C, heart rate above 90), immunocompromise, or deeper infection signs such as bullae, sloughing, hypotension, organ dysfunction
claims.quote: Severe infection: patients who have failed oral antibiotic treatment or those with systemic signs of infection such as temperature >38°C, tachycardia (heart rate >90 beats per minute), [...] bullae, skin sloughing, hypotension, or evidence of organ dysfunction

claims.text: IDSA framework organizes treatment by purulence, MRSA risk and severity (treatment intro sentence)
claims.quote: Mild infection: typical cellulitis/erysipelas with no focus of purulence. Moderate infection: typical cellulitis/erysipelas with systemic signs of infection.

claims.text: Routine blood and skin cultures not recommended; blood cultures generally positive in 5% or fewer of cases
claims.quote: Cultures of blood or cutaneous aspirates, biopsies, or swabs are not routinely recommended (strong, moderate). [...] Blood cultures are generally positive in ≤5% of cases [38].

claims.text: Blood cultures for patients with cancer, severe systemic features such as high fever and hypotension, or unusual predisposing factors (immersion injury, animal bites, neutropenia, severe cell-mediated immunodeficiency)
claims.quote: Blood cultures should be obtained and cultures of skin biopsy or aspirate considered for patients with malignancy, severe systemic features (such as high fever and hypotension),

claims.text: Severe infections: IV MRSA options (vancomycin, daptomycin, linezolid, telavancin); vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam or imipenem/meropenem as empiric regimen
claims.quote: include intravenous drugs (vancomycin, daptomycin, linezolid, or telavancin) [...] Vancomycin plus either piperacillin-tazobactam or imipenem/meropenem is recommended as a reasonable empiric regimen for severe infections (strong, moderate).

claims.text: Elevation hastens improvement via gravity drainage; elevation plus treatment of predisposing factors is a strong recommendation
claims.quote: Elevation of the affected area hastens improvement by promoting gravity drainage of edema and inflammatory substances. [...] Elevation of the affected area and treatment of predisposing factors, such as edema or underlying cutaneous disorders, are recommended (strong, moderate).

claims.text: Corticosteroids (prednisone 40 mg daily for 7 days) could be considered in nondiabetic adults; weak recommendation; trial of 108 nondiabetic adults showed faster resolution
claims.quote: Systemic corticosteroids (eg, prednisone 40 mg daily for 7 days) could be considered in nondiabetic adult patients with cellulitis (weak, moderate). [...] 108 adult nondiabetic patients, [...] significantly more rapid clinical resolution of cellulitis

claims.text: Prophylaxis for 3-4 episodes per year: oral penicillin or erythromycin twice daily for 4-52 weeks, or IM benzathine penicillin every 2-4 weeks (prevention section and FAQ)
claims.quote: Administration of prophylactic antibiotics, such as oral penicillin or erythromycin bid for 4–52 weeks, or intramuscular benzathine penicillin every 2–4 weeks, should be considered in patients who have 3–4 episodes of cellulitis per year

claims.text: Examine toe spaces in leg cellulitis; treating fissuring, scaling or maceration may reduce recurrent infection (key takeaway, tinea section)
claims.quote: In lower-extremity cellulitis, clinicians should carefully examine the interdigital toe spaces because treating fissuring, scaling, or maceration may eradicate colonization with pathogens and reduce the incidence of recurrent infection
